stem: A 22-year-old female college student has fever, cramps and bloody diarrhea that began 3 days after a backyard barbecue where chicken was served undercooked. Stool microscopy shows many leukocytes. A stool culture on selective medium at 42 C in a low-oxygen jar grows curved gram-negative rods.
oneliner: 22F + fever, cramps, bloody diarrhea 3 days after undercooked chicken + fecal leukocytes + curved gram-negative rods growing at 42 C → organism?
ask: Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

whyNot.B: Grows as **straight** rods; her culture shows **curved** gram-negative rods at **42 C**
whyNot.C: Gives **watery diarrhea** without fever or blood and has no **fecal leukocytes**; she has **fever and bloody stool**
whyNot.D: A **gram-positive** rod; she has **gram-negative curved rods**, **fever** and **bloody** stool
whyNot.E: Curved gram-negative rods too, but linked to **raw seafood**; she ate **chicken**

why: **Undercooked poultry**, fever, **bloody diarrhea with fecal leukocytes** and **curved gram-negative rods growing at 42 C in low oxygen** identify Campylobacter jejuni. It invades the colonic mucosa and can later trigger Guillain-Barre syndrome.

bug.name: Campylobacter jejuni
bug.type: Gram-negative curved (comma or S-shaped) rod, motile, microaerophilic
bug.lab: Oxidase positive; grows at 42 C on selective agar in low oxygen; stool shows leukocytes
bug.virulence: Invades colonic and ileal mucosa; surface lipo-oligosaccharide resembles nerve gangliosides (molecular mimicry)
bug.spread: Fecal-oral from undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk or contaminated water; animals and pets
bug.causes: Fever with bloody diarrhea and cramps; Guillain-Barre syndrome; reactive arthritis

idea.rule: Match the exposure to the diarrheal organism.
also: Undercooked poultry or eggs: Campylobacter and Salmonella
Raw or undercooked seafood: Vibrio parahaemolyticus

stem: A 34-year-old woman and four other guests at a catered buffet begin vomiting about 2 hours after the meal; she also has mild cramps. None has fever or bloody stool. The common dish was rice from a large pot that had sat on a warm tray since morning and was stir-fried just before serving. Everyone recovers within a day.
oneliner: 34F + four other guests + vomiting 2 hours after a buffet + no fever or blood + rice kept warm since morning, then stir-fried + recovery within a day → organism?
ask: Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: Also causes early vomiting, but is linked to **handled salty or creamy foods**; here the dish was **rice kept warm**
whyNot.B: Incubates about 8 to 16 hours and gives **watery diarrhea**; these guests **vomited at 2 hours**
whyNot.D: Linked to **raw seafood**; the common dish was **rice**
whyNot.E: Incubates about a day or two; these guests vomited **2 hours** after eating

why: **Vomiting within hours** after **rice held warm and then fried**, with **no fever** and recovery in a day, is Bacillus cereus food poisoning. Its spores survive cooking, and the **preformed heat-stable emetic toxin** is not destroyed by frying.

bug.name: Bacillus cereus
bug.lab: Beta-hemolytic on blood agar; motile, unlike B. anthracis; spores survive boiling and frying
bug.virulence: Heat-stable emetic toxin (cereulide) preformed in starchy food; heat-labile enterotoxin causes the diarrheal form
bug.spread: Spores from soil contaminate grains; they germinate when cooked rice is left warm; no person-to-person spread
bug.causes: Emetic food poisoning from reheated rice; diarrheal food poisoning from meats and sauces; rarely eye infection after trauma

idea.rule: A preformed toxin gives a short incubation, vomiting and no fever.
also: Staphylococcus aureus: 1 to 6 hours, from salty or creamy foods such as ham and custard
Clostridium perfringens: 8 to 16 hours, watery diarrhea from reheated meat
Bacillus cereus emetic form: reheated rice; diarrheal form: meats and sauces
Botulism: preformed neurotoxin from improperly canned food

stem: A 10-month-old boy who has not received any of his scheduled vaccines attends day care. In February he has 2 days of vomiting followed by profuse watery diarrhea and a low-grade fever. There is no blood in the stool and stool microscopy shows no leukocytes. The family has not traveled, and he has no cough, conjunctivitis or rash. His mucous membranes are dry, his eyes look sunken and he has had no wet diaper for 10 hours.
oneliner: 10-mo M + unvaccinated + day care in winter + vomiting then profuse watery diarrhea + low fever + no blood or leukocytes + no travel + dehydration → organism?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: Gives brief vomiting outbreaks at **all ages**; an **unvaccinated infant in day care** with **dehydrating watery diarrhea** points to the virus the infant vaccine prevents
whyNot.C: Enteric types cause a milder diarrhea, and he has **no cough or conjunctivitis**
whyNot.D: Typically follows **travel**; his family has **not traveled**
whyNot.E: Causes weeks of foul, greasy stools; his illness is **2 days of vomiting then watery diarrhea**

why: An **unvaccinated infant in day care in winter** with **vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, no blood or leukocytes** and **dehydration** fits rotavirus. It destroys mature villus-tip enterocytes, causing malabsorption plus secretion.

bug.name: Rotavirus
bug.lab: Diagnosed by stool antigen detection; 11 RNA segments allow reassortment
bug.virulence: Infects mature enterocytes at the villus tips; loss of absorptive cells plus the NSP4 enterotoxin give malabsorptive and secretory diarrhea
bug.spread: Fecal-oral with a very small infectious dose; day care; winter and spring
bug.causes: Severe watery diarrhea with vomiting and dehydration in infants; prevented by a live oral vaccine

idea.rule: Match the diarrhea to the age, season and setting.
also: Norovirus: outbreaks on cruise ships and in schools, all ages
Adenovirus types 40 and 41: milder gastroenteritis in young children
Giardia: campers and day care, foul greasy stools over weeks
Enterotoxigenic E. coli: watery traveler's diarrhea
